title: A Guide to Contingencies in a California Purchase Agreement
content_html:
When you make an offer on a home in California, the purchase agreement isn't just a price and a closing date — it's a set of conditions that have to be satisfied before the deal becomes final. Those conditions are called contingencies, and understanding how they work is one of the most important parts of navigating a purchase with confidence. This guide walks through the standard contingencies you'll encounter, how they're typically structured, and what it means when you "remove" one.

What a Contingency Actually Does

A contingency is a condition in the purchase agreement that must be met, or affirmatively waived, for the contract to move forward as written. If a contingency isn't satisfied and isn't waived, the buyer generally has the right to cancel the transaction and, depending on the specific contingency and the timing, recover their earnest money deposit. Contingencies exist to give both sides a structured way to investigate the property, line up financing, and confirm the details of the transaction before money and title actually change hands.

Most California purchase agreements built on the standard association forms include a handful of contingencies as the default, with a set number of days assigned to each. Buyers and sellers can negotiate those timeframes as part of the offer — which is one reason it pays to think through contingencies carefully before you write an offer rather than after. Our guide to making a competitive offer covers how contingency terms factor into offer strategy.

The Loan Contingency

If you're financing your purchase, the loan contingency protects you if you're unable to secure the mortgage described in your offer. It gives you a window of time to work with your lender to finalize loan approval. If financing falls through despite a good-faith effort and you cancel within the contingency period, you're generally in a position to have your deposit returned. Once you remove this contingency, though, you're telling the seller you're confident financing will close — so it's worth doing only when your lender has actually confirmed you're clear to close, not just because a deadline is approaching.

The Appraisal Contingency

Lenders require an appraisal to confirm the home is worth at least what they're lending against it. The appraisal contingency protects you if the appraised value comes in below the purchase price. If that happens, you typically have options: renegotiate the price with the seller, cover the gap in cash, or cancel and get your deposit back, depending on how the contingency is written and whether it's still active. In competitive markets, some buyers waive this contingency or cap how much they'll cover — a decision worth discussing carefully, since waiving it means you'd be on the hook for the full gap if the appraisal comes in low.

The Inspection Contingency

This is usually the buyer's main opportunity to have the property physically inspected and to request repairs, a price adjustment, or credits — or to cancel the contract entirely if the inspection turns up something you're not willing to live with. It's a broad contingency, covering everything from the general condition of the structure to things like pest activity, roof condition, or plumbing and electrical systems. For a deeper look at what this process actually involves, see our home inspection guide for first-time buyers.

The Title Contingency

Before closing, a title company researches the property's ownership history to confirm the seller can legally transfer clear title. The title contingency gives the buyer a chance to review the preliminary title report and object to anything problematic — an old lien, an easement you weren't expecting, a boundary dispute — before moving forward.

The Seller Disclosures Contingency

California sellers are generally expected to disclose known material facts about a property's condition as part of the transaction. The disclosures contingency gives buyers time to review those documents — the statutory disclosure forms, any known defects, and other seller-provided information — and to cancel if something in them changes their view of the property. Our article on seller disclosure requirements goes into more detail on what sellers typically provide.

The Sale of Buyer's Existing Home

If you need to sell a current home to fund the purchase of a new one, this contingency ties the new purchase to the successful — or at least pending — sale of your existing property. It's less common in competitive markets, since sellers often prefer offers that aren't dependent on another sale, but it can be an important tool if you genuinely need the proceeds from your current home to move forward.

HOA Document Review

If the property is part of a homeowners association, buyers are typically given a period to review HOA governing documents, financial statements, and rules before the purchase becomes unconditional. This overlaps conceptually with general due diligence but is often treated as its own item given how much can be buried in HOA paperwork. See our guide to HOA fees before you buy for what to look for.

How Removing a Contingency Works

"Removing" a contingency means formally notifying the other party, usually in writing, that the condition has been satisfied or that you're choosing to proceed without it. Once a contingency is removed, your ability to cancel the contract based on that particular issue — and still expect your deposit back — is generally much more limited. This is why buyers should treat contingency removal deadlines seriously: reviewing loan status, inspection results, disclosures, and title before signing off, rather than letting a deadline pass by default.

It's also worth understanding that contingencies and deadlines are negotiable at the time an offer is written. A seller may ask for shorter contingency periods to move the transaction along faster, and a buyer in a competitive market might voluntarily shorten them, or waive certain contingencies altogether, to make an offer more appealing. Every one of these decisions carries real risk trade-offs, so it's worth thinking through what you're comfortable waiving and what you're not before you're under time pressure mid-transaction.

Contingencies and Escrow

Contingency periods run concurrently with the broader escrow process — the neutral third-party process that handles funds, documents, and instructions between buyer and seller until closing. Understanding how these two things interact helps make sense of why certain deadlines fall where they do. Our guide to what happens during escrow walks through that timeline in more detail.

Working With Your Agent on Contingency Strategy

There's no one-size-fits-all approach to contingencies. A buyer with strong financing and a flexible timeline might be comfortable waiving certain protections to strengthen an offer, while a buyer without much room for surprises should generally keep contingencies intact and use the time they provide. Discuss your specific situation, market conditions, and risk tolerance with your real estate agent before writing an offer, and don't hesitate to ask questions about what a given contingency does and doesn't cover as you move through the transaction.
